title: Hip Level
description: A hip-level shot sits the camera around belt or holster height so hands, gait, and weapons share the plane of focus. It is a height choice, usually with a level horizon: the hands will decide.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: Westerns minted it because a draw happens at the belt. The face is still in the upper frame, but the story is in the fingers, the buckle, the coat hem at the wrist.
Tension reads before anyone looks up. Crime films stole the height for a gun that might come out during a talk.
It is not a Cowboy Shot, which is a frame size from mid-thigh up and can be taken from eye height. It is not a Low Angle unless you also pitch up.
Hip-level can stay level and still make the holster the equator of the picture.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Pedestal to belt height on a standing adult (roughly 90 to 110 cm). Keep roll level.
A slight look-up is optional; a true hip-level often aims through the hands toward the far figure. Depth of field should hold the holster and the facing body.
A wider lens at this height will stretch legs; a longer lens compresses the standoff. Prompt: hip-level camera, gunbelt height, hands and holster in the plane of focus.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it when the hands will decide: a standoff, a pocketed weapon, a key passed at waist height. Concrete beat: two standing figures, belts in a line, fingers idle near leather.
Do not use it when the face is the only event; rise to Shoulder Level or Eye Level.

sections.title: Compared with similar shots

blocks.text: Cowboy Shot crops mid-thigh as a size; hip-level is where the lens sits. Ground Level is on the dirt and privileges boots.
Low Angle pitches up for monument. Shoulder Level is a walking companion, closer to the face.
Eye Level ignores the belt.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly keeps holsters and hands alive in the line of the lens during standoffs. No Country for Old Men works at belt and pocket height so a captured bolt pistol is as present as a face.
Borrow the height of the hands, not a copied desert.

sections.title: Prompt it

blocks.text: Name belt height, not low camera. Quote: Hip-level camera on [Subject], gunbelt height, Western stance, hands and holster in the plane of focus.
Add: horizon through the hands, level roll, face still in the upper frame, not a worm's-eye, not mid-thigh crop unless you also want a cowboy size.
Hip-level camera on [Subject], gunbelt height, Western stance, hands and holster in the plane of focus.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is a Low Angle power tilt or a Cowboy Shot from standing eye height. Tell: nostrils and ceiling, or a mid-thigh crop taken from above the chest.
Fix: camera at belt, looking through the hands, horizon level. If only boots are sharp, you dropped to Ground Level.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is hip level in film?
A hip-level shot places the camera at belt or holster height. Hands, gait, and weapons sit in the plane of focus; the face remains in the upper frame.
Hip level vs cowboy shot
Hip level is camera height at the belt. A cowboy shot is a frame size from mid-thigh up. You can combine them, but a cowboy can also be taken from eye height.
When should I use hip level?
Use it when hands and a possible draw are the beat. Do not use it for a seated talk or a face that needs to fill the frame.
How do I prompt hip level for AI image or video?
Write: Hip-level camera on [Subject], gunbelt height, hands and holster in the plane of focus, horizon through the hands, not a low-angle tilt.
